component orders","Medication and transfusion history, prior reactions, allergies, and code status/goals of care"],"priorityActions":["With the transfusion already stopped, maintain the IV line with new tubing and infuse 0.9% sodium chloride wide open for aggressive isotonic volume resuscitation to restore perfusion and maintain renal blood flow and urine output, escalating to vasopressor support per order if hypotension persists; do not flush the residual blood in the existing tubing into the client","Immediately notify the provider and the blood bank, initiate the transfusion-reaction protocol by returning the unit and tubing and sending clerical recheck plus post-reaction blood and urine specimens (DAT, repeat type and crossmatch, plasma-free hemoglobin, CBC, coagulation studies), and obtain and administer ordered blood component replacement for DIC (cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen for fibrinogen 140 mg/dL, FFP for INR 1.8 and aPTT 52 seconds, platelets as indicated)"],"reasoning":"Onset within 12 minutes of starting RBCs with fever, rigors, bilateral flank pain, hypotension, hemoglobinuria, and a sense of impending doom is the classic presentation of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility. The laboratory picture confirms brisk intravascular hemolysis: LDH 1,840 U/L, bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, and haptoglobin <10 mg/dL with port-wine urine. Progression 30 minutes after stopping the transfusion — falling platelets (104), fibrinogen 140 mg/dL, INR 1.8, aPTT 52 seconds, and oozing from puncture sites — is consumptive coagulopathy (DIC) triggered by the hemolytic reaction, while worsening hypotension with oliguria and pigmented urine signals hemoglobin-mediated acute kidney injury. Because the transfusion has already been stopped, the next priorities are hemodynamic and renal rescue (isotonic fluids through fresh tubing, vasopressors if needed) and simultaneous activation of the transfusion-reaction pathway with provider/blood bank notification, specimen and unit return, and factor/platelet replacement for the DIC. Monitoring therefore centers on the two organ systems failing in real time: renal perfusion (hourly urine output and color, MAP, BUN/creatinine, potassium) and the coagulation/hemolysis trajectory (fibrinogen, platelets, INR/aPTT, D-dimer, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, plus bleeding assessment).","stage1Confidence":"high","stemEvidence":[{"stemFact":"Fever, rigors, bilateral flank pain, hypotension, and a sense of impending doom within 12 minutes of starting a red blood cell transfusion","target":"condition"},{"stemFact":"Hemoglobinuria and port-wine urine with LDH 1,840 U/L, bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, and haptoglobin <10 mg/dL indicating intravascular hemolysis","target":"condition"},{"stemFact":"Platelets 104 ×10³/µL, fibrinogen 140 mg/dL, INR 1.8, aPTT 52 seconds, and oozing from puncture sites indicating consumptive coagulopathy","target":"condition"},{"stemFact":"Worsening hypotension 30 minutes after the transfusion was stopped","target":"priorityAction1"},{"stemFact":"Oliguria with port-wine urine reflecting hemoglobin-induced renal injury requiring flow and perfusion support","target":"priorityAction1"},{"stemFact":"Acute reaction to a red blood cell transfusion requiring transfusion-reaction protocol, unit and specimen return, and clerical/ABO verification","target":"priorityAction2"},{"stemFact":"Fibrinogen 140 mg/dL, INR 1.8, aPTT 52 seconds, platelets 104 ×10³/µL, and oozing from puncture sites requiring ordered component replacement","target":"priorityAction2"},{"stemFact":"Oliguria with port-wine urine and worsening hypotension","target":"evaluationParameter1"},{"stemFact":"Hemoglobinuria from ongoing intravascular hemolysis threatening renal tubular function","target":"evaluationParameter1"},{"stemFact":"Platelets 104 ×10³/µL, fibrinogen 140 mg/dL, INR 1.8, aPTT 52 seconds","target":"evaluationParameter2"},{"stemFact":"Oozing from puncture sites with LDH 1,840 U/L, bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, and haptoglobin <10 mg/dL","target":"evaluationParameter2"}]}
